challenges.name: spec-and-tests-first-quiz
challenges.title: What do the acceptance tests prove?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the second attempt at lesson bookmarks: the agent's add() next to the acceptance tests it passed, and a test that was run against a stub before any code was written.

questions.explanation: False. The code checks the limit before it checks for a duplicate, so a user at 50 bookmarks gets "limit_reached" for a lesson they already saved, and the app tells them to delete bookmarks to save something that is already saved. None of the five tests puts both rules in play at once: the duplicate test runs with one bookmark, the limit test with 50 different lessons. Tests prove exactly the cases they contain. The fix is a sixth acceptance test for the interaction (50 bookmarks, re-add one of them) and a spec that states the order of the checks. The misconception is that "every spec rule has a passing test" means "the spec is implemented": rules interact, and each interaction you care about needs its own case.

True. The red run proves the assertion is wired up: it ran, it compared a real value, and it rejected a wrong one. With the test file unchanged (git diff confirms it), the only thing that can turn it green is the implementation. A test that has never been seen failing could be green for the wrong reason: a wrong import, an assertion that is never reached, an expectation copied from the code's own output. That is why the habit is to watch every acceptance test fail against a stub before you hand the task to the agent. The misconception is that a red test before implementation is wasted time; it is the cheapest proof that the test can catch a mistake.

challenges.name: bookmark-service-from-spec
challenges.title: Implement lesson bookmarks from a spec
challenges.description:
CodeDev learners want to bookmark lessons and find them again on their dashboard. The first attempt was built by an agent from a one-line prompt and shipped with duplicate bookmarks, no limit and the oldest bookmark first. This time the spec came first. Implement the in-memory class BookmarkService(lessonIds) with three methods.

add(userId, lessonId, at) runs these checks in this order and returns the first that applies: (1) "invalid_request" when userId or lessonId is not a string with at least one non-space character, or at is not a finite number; (2) "lesson_not_found" when lessonId is not one of the catalog's lessonIds (exact match, case-sensitive); (3) "already_bookmarked" when this user already has this lesson (nothing changes, the original time is kept); (4) "limit_reached" when the user already has 50 bookmarks; otherwise the bookmark is saved with time at and the result is "added".

remove(userId, lessonId) returns "invalid_request" for an invalid userId or lessonId (same rule), "removed" when the user had that bookmark (it is deleted), and "not_bookmarked" otherwise, also for a lesson that is not in the catalog. Removing twice is not an error.

list(userId) returns the user's lesson ids, most recent first: larger at first; for the same at, the bookmark added later comes first. at is a time in milliseconds from the client and does not always increase (the mobile app syncs offline bookmarks late). A user with no bookmarks gets []. Limits and bookmarks are per user.

Input (stdin, read by the test runner): { "lessons": string[], "commands": [...] } where each command is { "op": "add", userId, lessonId, at }, { "op": "remove", userId, lessonId } or { "op": "list", userId }. All commands run in order on one service. Output: one JSON array with the result of every command (a string for add and remove, an array of lesson ids for list). Up to 1,000 commands, 120 lessons and 40 users per test; invalid input arrives as it would from a client (empty or blank strings, null, a number sent as a string). You may use an AI assistant: give it this spec and write the acceptance tests first. The hidden tests check every rule and how the rules interact.
hints: For each sentence of the spec, which input would break it? Then look for places where two rules meet: what should a user who already has 50 bookmarks get when they bookmark a lesson that is already in their list?

Look at three places: the order of the checks in add (the spec numbers them), what you store per bookmark (the time at is not enough to tell two bookmarks with the same at apart, so keep their arrival order too), and the comparator in list, which needs a second key for equal times. For invalid input, check the type of each value, not only whether it is empty.

A similar spec on different data: a course wishlist with at most 3 courses per user. After adding c1 at 10, c2 at 10 and c3 at 5, the list is c2, c1, c3 (same time: the later arrival first; c3 is older). Adding c4 now returns full, but adding c2 again returns exists, because the duplicate check runs before the size check. Removing c9, which was never added, returns not_in_wishlist and changes nothing.

tests.name: Add three lessons, list them newest first, then remove one
Adding a bookmark twice keeps one; a second remove is not an error
Limit of 50 per user: the 51st fails, a re-add at the limit is not a limit error
Invalid input and unknown lessons: invalid_request, lesson_not_found, not_bookmarked
Same timestamp: the bookmark added later comes first
Order follows at, not arrival: a late offline sync and a re-add after remove
Large input: 40 users, 1,000 random commands, then every list
